messages.subject: How is the general structure to fit a nested random effect?
parts:
I am trying to fit a Poisson with nested random effect for study purposes. I already managed to fit a model with random intercept only based on this code. So I tried to adapt it for a nested structure, but I haven't figured out how to do it. If anyone could provide a general example I would be glad to.

Anyway, I will post what I have got so far:
// Poisson Regression with Nested Random Effects
#include <TMB.hpp>
template<class Type>
Type objective_function<Type>::operator() ()
{
  // Data provided from user
  DATA_VECTOR(Y);
  DATA_MATRIX(X);
  DATA_IVECTOR(ID);
  DATA_IVECTOR(IDB);
  // Parameters of the model
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(b0);    // overall mean
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(bi);    // sample units i = 0,1,2,3
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(bij);   // block inside sample units ij = 0,1,2,3, ... , 20
  PARAMETER(tau);
  PARAMETER(sigma);
  Type nll = 0;
  tau = exp(tau);
  sigma = exp(sigma);
 
  // Probability of bi (sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bi,  0, 1/sigma, true));   // ua = 4
  // Probability of bij (block in sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bij, 0,   1/tau, true));   // bij size 20 (ua = 4 * bloco = 5)
 
  int n = Y.size();
  vector<Type> eta(n);
  eta = X*b0;
 
  // Probability of yi
  for (int i=0; i<n; i++){
    // nll -= dpois(Y(i), exp(eta(i)+ bij(IDB(i)))  , true); // b0 + bi + bij
    nll -= dpois(Y(i), exp(eta(i) + bi(ID(i)) + bij(IDB(i))), true); // b0 + bi + bij
  }
  return nll;
}


I also tried to change the middle part of the code (two dnorm) by the following:
  DATA_VECTOR(mubi);
  DATA_VECTOR(mubij);
  int count = -1;
  int nbi = bi.size();
  int nbij = bij.size()/nbi;
  for (int i=0; i<nbi; i++){
    // Probability of bi (sample units)
    nll = -dnorm(bi(i), mubi(i), 1/sigma, true);   // ua = 4
    for (int j=0; j<nbij; j++){
      // Probability of bij (block in sample units)
      count += 1;
      nll = -dnorm(bij(count), mubij(count),   1/tau, true);   // bij size 20 (ua = 4 * bloco = 5)
    }
  }

but it didn't work either. In the first case, the code compiles, but sigma doesn't change along the compilation. In the second, it also compiles, however my objective function acts even more weird. (I also attached my R code). I know that the  main problem is with the block in sample units, but I don't know how to fix it.

This is how the model is written:

Y_ijk ∼ P (λ_ijk)
g(λ_ijk) = ( β_0 + b_i ) + b_i:j
b_i ∼ N( 0, σ^2 ); b_i:j ∼ N (0,τ^2 )

Thanks in advance if anyone can help.

messages.author: 02e03030784aa6a7
messages.subject: Re: How is the general structure to fit a nested random effect?
parts:
You can use model.matrix(y~x+x*z,...) in R to create a design matrix X.
Then you send X to the .cpp file and evaluate the linear predictor X*beta there.
This a completely general approach, and switches the problem from C++ to R (which is good for this task)

If you have factors with many levels it may be necessary to let X be of sparse matrix type.

Hans

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] How is the general structure to fit a nested random effect?
parts: Nested random effects aren’t really special in this context. You seem to be adding them in Ok here
nll -= dpois(Y(i), exp(eta(i) + bi(ID(i)) + bij(IDB(i))), true); // b0 + bi + bij

, but you’re using the variance parameters incorrectly. 

Instead of

PARAMETER(tau);
  PARAMETER(sigma);
  Type nll = 0;
  tau = exp(tau);
  sigma = exp(sigma);
  
  // Probability of bi (sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bi,  0, 1/sigma, true));   // ua = 4
  // Probability of bij (block in sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bij, 0,   1/tau, true));   // bij size 20 (ua = 4 * bloco = 5)

You should have something like

  PARAMETER(logtau);
  PARAMETER(logsigma);
  Type nll = 0;
  Type tau = exp(logtau);
  Type sigma = exp(logsigma);
// Probability of bi (sample units)
nll = -sum(dnorm(bi,  Type(0), sigma, true));   // ua = 4
// Probability of bij (block in sample units)

nll = -sum(dnorm(bij, Type(0),   tau, true));   // bij size 20 (ua = 4 * bloco = 5)

Does that fix it?

cheers,
Mollie

On Thursday, 30 April 2020 05:47:11 UTC-3, Mollie Brooks wrote:
Nested random effects aren’t really special in this context. You seem to be adding them in Ok here
    nll -= dpois(Y(i), exp(eta(i) + bi(ID(i)) + bij(IDB(i))), true); // b0 + bi + bij

, but you’re using the variance parameters incorrectly. 

Instead of 
  PARAMETER(tau);
  PARAMETER(sigma);
  Type nll = 0;
  tau = exp(tau);
  sigma = exp(sigma);
  
  // Probability of bi (sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bi,  0, 1/sigma, true));   // ua = 4
  // Probability of bij (block in sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bij, 0,   1/tau, true));   // bij size 20 (ua = 4 * bloco = 5)

You should have something like

  PARAMETER(logtau);
  PARAMETER(logsigma);
  Type nll = 0;
  Type tau = exp(logtau);
  Type sigma = exp(logsigma);
  
  // Probability of bi (sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bi,  Type(0), sigma, true));   // ua = 4
  // Probability of bij (block in sample units)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(bij, Type(0),   tau, true));   // bij size 20 (ua = 4 * bloco = 5)

Does that fix it?

cheers,
Mollie

On 30Apr 2020, at 9:58, Hans Skaug <hsk...@gmail.com> wrote:

You can use model.matrix(y~x+x*z,...) in R to create a design matrix X.
Then you send X to the .cpp file and evaluate the linear predictor X*beta there.
This a completely general approach, and switches the problem from C++ to R (which is good for this task)

If you have factors with many levels it may be necessary to let X be of sparse matrix type.

Hans
